subject: Mathematics
status: DRAFT — for review by a Mathematics teacher before it is relied on
source: Drafted against NCERT Class IX Mathematics 'Ganita Manjari' Part 1 (iemh1) and the 497 questions imported from C:/dev/sirah_project/NCERT/data. Many of those questions are older NCERT and exemplar items mapped into the new book's chapters — Heron's formula in Chapter 6, circle theorems in Chapter 5 — so the outcomes cover what the questions test as well as what the new chapter titles announce.
notes: Prerequisites link several of these concepts to the Class 10 concepts they prepare for, so a Class 10 gap can name a Class 9 root cause.

outcomes.statement: Identifies the abscissa and ordinate of a point, and the quadrant or axis on which a point lies from the signs of its coordinates.
Uses coordinates to plot points and to find a missing vertex of a figure whose sides are parallel to the axes.
Calculates the distance between two points on a horizontal or vertical line from their coordinates.
Applies Pythagoras' theorem to calculate the distance of a point from the origin, or between two points, and compares distances.

concepts.name: Plotting points on the coordinate plane

outcomes.statement: Calculates the value of a linear or quadratic polynomial for a given value of the variable.
Identifies a linear equation in two variables, writes its solutions, and describes the graph of equations such as y = 6.
Writes a linear rule y = ax + b for a growing pattern or a situation such as a bill with a fixed and a variable charge, and uses it to predict.
Solves word problems about numbers, lengths, coins and costs by forming and solving a linear equation.
Classifies a number as rational or irrational, and explains why every rational number has a terminating or recurring decimal expansion.
Converts between fractions and decimal expansions, including writing a recurring or terminating decimal as a fraction in lowest terms.
Uses factorisation to write a surd such as √75 in its simplest form, and rationalises a denominator such as 1/(√7 − 2).
Applies the laws of exponents to simplify expressions with integral and rational powers.
Applies the identities for (a ± b)² and (a + b)(a − b) to expand expressions and to calculate squares such as 96².
Applies the identities for (a ± b)³ to expand cubes.
Uses an identity to find a² + b² or a³ + b³ from the values of a + b and ab.
Uses splitting the middle term and the identities to factorise quadratic expressions such as x² − 8x + 12.
Applies the fact that the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord to calculate a chord's length, its distance from the centre, or the radius.
Relates equal chords to equal angles at the centre and to equal distances from the centre.
Applies the theorem that the angle an arc subtends at the centre is double the angle it subtends at the circle.
Uses the facts that angles in the same segment are equal and the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
Applies the property that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.

concepts.name: Chords and their distance from the centre
Angles subtended by arcs and cyclic quadrilaterals

topics.title: Perimeter and area of plane figures

outcomes.statement: Calculates the perimeter and area of squares, rectangles, parallelograms and triangles from their sides and heights.
Calculates the circumference and area of a circle or a semicircle, and a radius from a given area or circumference.
Explains why a median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area, and finds areas of figures formed by joining mid-points.
Applies Heron's formula to calculate the area of a triangle from its three sides, including equilateral and isosceles triangles.

concepts.name: Area and perimeter of plane figures

outcomes.statement: Lists the sample space of an experiment such as rolling a die or tossing coins, including by drawing a tree diagram.
Calculates the experimental probability of an event from recorded trials, and distinguishes it from theoretical probability.
Calculates the theoretical probability of an event with equally likely outcomes, and the probability that an event does not happen.
Writes the explicit rule and the recursive rule for a sequence, and uses either to find a term.
Identifies whether a sequence is arithmetic, geometric or neither, and recognises special sequences such as triangular numbers.
Uses the rule of an arithmetic progression to find a term, or to decide whether a number is a term.
Calculates the common ratio and a given term of a geometric progression.
Calculates the sum of the first n natural numbers, and finds n for a given sum.

concepts.name: Explicit and recursive rules for sequences
